svg.title: A container is just a Linux process — these are the fences around it, from the outside in

g.text: A container is just a Linux process — these are the fences around it, from the outside in
THE PROBLEM
1 · WHO the process is — securityContext
2 · WHICH root powers it keeps — Linux capabilities
3 · WHICH system calls it may make — seccomp
4 · WHICH files and resources it may touch — AppArmor / SELinux (MAC)
5 · WHO root really is — user namespaces
6 · WHOSE kernel it uses — sandboxed runtimes (gVisor, Kata Containers)
Every container on a node shares ONE Linux kernel. A process asks the kernel for everything — open a file,
open a socket, load a module, change the clock — through about 300+ SYSTEM CALLS. If an attacker controls the
process, every kernel feature it can reach is attack surface. Each fence below shrinks what the process can ask for.
Namespaces and cgroups (chapter 03) decide what a container can SEE and how much it can USE. These decide what it may DO.
runAsUser: 1000 · runAsNonRoot: true · allowPrivilegeEscalation: false · readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
privileged: true
turns almost every fence below OFF — the container gets nearly the same access as the host.
hostNetwork / hostPID / hostIPC: true put the container in the HOST's namespaces — it sees every process or interface on the node.
Linux splits 'root' into ~40 separate powers: NET_ADMIN (reconfigure networking), SYS_ADMIN (mount, and much more),
SYS_TIME (set the clock), NET_BIND_SERVICE (bind ports below 1024)...
capabilities: {drop: [ALL], add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE]} — so even a process running as root inside the container is
a root with almost no powers. The restricted Pod Security Standard requires drop ALL.
Secure computing mode: a kernel filter on system calls.
A profile is an allow-list; a forbidden call fails
(or kills the process) before the kernel does any work.
seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault (the container runtime's sensible default — blocks dozens of risky calls)
Localhost (your own profile file on the node) · Unconfined (no filter — the historical default)
Analogy: a bank teller who will only process the 50 transaction types on their list, whatever the customer says.
Mandatory Access Control
: the KERNEL enforces a policy that even root cannot override — unlike ordinary file
permissions, which the owner (or root) can change at will.
AppArmor (Ubuntu, Debian, SUSE): a PROFILE of paths — 'may read /etc/nginx, may never write /proc/sys'.
securityContext.appArmorProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault} (a field since v1.30; annotations before)
SELinux (RHEL, Fedora): LABELS on every process and file, with rules about which labels may access which.
seccomp asks 'which kernel functions?'; MAC asks 'on which objects?'. They are layered, not alternatives.
spec.hostUsers: false — UID 0 INSIDE the container is mapped to an unprivileged UID (say 165536) on the HOST.
The process still believes it is root, and can do root things inside its own namespace — but if it escapes the container,
it lands on the node as a nobody. Alpha v1.28 → beta v1.30 → stable v1.36.
gVisor
(runsc) puts a user-space 'application kernel' between the container and the host kernel, intercepting
system calls itself.
Kata Containers
runs each Pod inside a lightweight VM with its own kernel.
Selected per Pod with a RuntimeClass: spec.runtimeClassName: gvisor. Stronger isolation for untrusted code,
at a cost in performance and compatibility — so it is used selectively, not everywhere.
No single fence is enough, and each one covers a gap in the others: a non-root user with no capabilities, a syscall allow-list, a file-access policy, a fake root,
and — for untrusted workloads — a separate kernel. The restricted Pod Security Standard is, in effect, a checklist of fences 1 to 3.
